calls.head: The Senators like Halliday’s line against Suniev’s
calls.body: At home, the Senators keep sending Halliday’s line (Blais, Halliday and Cousins) out against opponents’ fourth lines, far more often than chance would suggest. Travis Green keeps choosing line for line. Tonight the Flames’ fourth line is Tsyplakov, Castagna and Suniev.

calls.head: The Senators should drive the play
calls.body: The Senators have been one of the league’s best at controlling the chances at 5-on-5, and the Flames near the bottom. Expect the Senators to spend more of the night in the Flames’ end. That’s about the puck, not the scoreboard: goalies and finishing decide plenty of games the chances don’t.

surprises.head: Both teams played to type
surprises.body: Nothing in this game strayed far from how these two usually play: the shot share, the quality of chances, special teams, hitting, ice time and goaltending all landed inside their normal night-to-night range.

story.head: The Senators squeak past the Flames
paras: Michael Amadio opened the scoring for the Senators midway through the first. Shane Pinto made it 2-0 late in the period, and that one stood up as the winner. The Flames’ Morgan Frost left late in the second period and didn’t return. The next day, he was listed as day to day with an upper-body injury. Joel Hanley and Pinto squared off midway through the third. Matt Coronato cut Ottawa’s lead to 2-1 on the power play with less than five minutes left.

The Flames outshot the Senators 36-31, but the Senators’ chances were the more dangerous ones. Linus Ullmark made 35 saves for the Senators, and Devin Cooley, who gave up five goals in Anaheim in his last start, kept the Flames in it, stopping 29 of 31. Ullmark has won six straight starts. The Sens moved to 16-6-3, still first in the Atlantic, while the Flames fell to 10-13-2, slipping to sixth in the Pacific.
